newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran needs better world ties for economic boost.
newsitem.headline: Iran needs better world ties for economic boost.

text.p: Iran has to improve ties with the West to attract foreign capital essential for the success of President Mohammad Khatami's call for an economic revival, analysts said on Tuesday.
But they predicted tough resistance by hardliners to speedy moves to open up to the West and much-needed foreign investment to tackle unemployment and inflation.
"We are obliged to open the door and have foreign capital come in," said businessman Amir Amini, a senior adviser at the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries and Mines.
"We, the state and the private sector, do not have the money to invest and create jobs," said Amini.
Inflation and unemployment are estimated by economists at double the official figures of 23 and 10 percent respectively.
Even if Khatami succeeded in solving sufficient problems with Western Europe to attract investments he would still face resistance from conservatives in parliament to any relaxation of the rules.
"Very simply they have to amend the constitution. It 'absolutely forbids' foreign involvement in so many fields," said one Iranian businessman who advocates drastic changes.

Khatami "has to do what he said he would do for the economy to start improving but it is very difficult...more on the internal front" than convincing Western powers to cooperate with Tehran, Amini said.

He was referring to Khatami's inaugural speech on Monday in which he sent conciliatory signals to the West, expressing a desire to cooperate with the rest of the world on the basis of mutual respect for the traditions, religion and system of rule in each country.
The hardline newspaper Kayhan International said on Tuesday Khatami's call for detente did not include Iran's declared enemy the United States.
Washington calls Iran a "rogue" state and has imposed a series of sanctions against it, including measures to keep non-U.S. capital out of Iran's vital oil sector.
Diplomats agree that any attempts by Khatami to even explore the possibility of a direct dialogue with Washington early in his presidency could be political suicide.

They say Khatami would first have to consolidate his power and use the overwhelming mandate handed him at the election in May to bring about a gradual easing in the Islamic system headed by supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Diplomats expect the first test of Khatami's future dealings with conservatives and hardliners to come when he puts forward his cabinet for parliamentary approval.
"They are watching out for any sign he is too liberal, moving too far too soon to create a symbolic issue to trip him," one diplomat said.
The parliament is led by speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri -- the conservative who many had expected to win the election.
Conservatives are already up in arms, slamming some of the likely cabinet ministers.

Among the targets is Ataollah Mohajerani who has been named as a possible minister of culture and Islamic guidance. He came under severe attack in the late 1980s for proposing direct talks with the United States.

The culture ministry "is in fact the command headquarters against the enemy's cultural invasion and therefore it should not be taken over by cowards or those who do not hold a grudge against America in their hearts," the hardline Jomhouri Eslami said in an editorial.
It did not name Mohajerani but said this "includes those who had proposed direct talks with America".

One Iranian businessman asked: "Why should the West be our 'enemy'? Like Khatami said, the governments must respect each other and if people here or there want to chant 'Death to America' or 'Death to Iran' or 'death' to this or that let them do that but not the governments."
